text: Algorithms and Data Structures: Graph Traversal and Shortest Paths Dijkstra's Algorithm is a fundamental single-source shortest path algorithm designed for weighted directed or undirected graphs with non-negative edge weights. The algorithm operates by maintaining a set of vertices whose final shortest-path weights from the source have already been determined. At each step, Dijkstra's algorithm greedily selects the vertex with the minimum tentative distance from the priority queue (commonly implemented using a Fibonacci heap or binary min-heap) and relaxes all of its outgoing edges. The relaxation step for an edge (u, v) with weight w(u, v) checks whether the current distance to v satisfies: if dist[v] > dist[u] + w(u, v), then dist[v] is updated to dist[u] + w(u, v). The time complexity of Dijkstra's algorithm implemented with a binary min-heap is O((V + E) log V), where V is the number of vertices and E is the number of edges. If implemented with a Fibonacci heap, the running time improves to O(E + V log V).

subject: algorithms
text: Limitations with Negative Edge Weights and Bellman-Ford Dijkstra's algorithm strictly fails when a graph contains negative edge weights. The core greedy invariant assumes that once a vertex is extracted from the priority queue, its shortest path distance is permanently finalized and cannot be decreased by any subsequent paths. When negative edge weights exist, a longer path with a negative edge could yield a smaller total path weight after the vertex has already been settled, violating the optimality invariant. To solve the single-source shortest path problem on graphs with negative edge weights, the Bellman-Ford algorithm must be used instead. The Bellman-Ford algorithm runs in O(V * E) time and operates by relaxing all edges in the graph V - 1 times. Furthermore, Bellman-Ford can detect the presence of negative-weight cycles reachable from the source: if an additional relaxation step in the V-th iteration still decreases any vertex distance, a negative-weight cycle exists.

text: Dynamic Programming and the 0/1 Knapsack Problem Dynamic programming is an algorithmic design paradigm based on the principle of optimality, where an optimal solution to an instance of a problem contains within it optimal solutions to subproblems. The two canonical properties required for dynamic programming to apply are optimal substructure and overlapping subproblems. In the 0/1 Knapsack Problem, we are given n items, each with a positive weight w_i and value v_i, and a knapsack of maximum capacity W. The objective is to select a subset of items to maximize total value without exceeding capacity W. Because each item can either be taken (1) or left behind (0), a simple greedy strategy based on value-to-weight ratio fails. The recurrence relation is defined over a 2D table DP[i][w]: if w_i <= w, DP[i][w] = max(DP[i-1][w], DP[i-1][w - w_i] + v_i); otherwise DP[i][w] = DP[i-1][w]. The time complexity is O(n * W), which is pseudo-polynomial in nature.

subject: automata
text: Theory of Computation: Finite Automata and Regular Languages A Deterministic Finite Automaton (DFA) is formally defined as a 5-tuple (Q, Sigma, delta, q_0, F), where Q is a finite set of states, Sigma is a finite alphabet of input symbols, delta is the transition function mapping Q x Sigma to Q, q_0 in Q is the initial start state, and F subset of Q is the set of accept (or final) states. DFAs recognize the class of regular languages. A Non-Deterministic Finite Automaton (NFA) differs in its transition function, which maps Q x (Sigma union {epsilon}) to the power set 2^Q, allowing state transitions on empty strings (epsilon transitions) or multiple possible subsequent states for a single symbol. Despite this flexibility, the subset construction algorithm proves that NFAs and DFAs have equivalent computational power: any NFA with n states can be converted to an equivalent DFA with at most 2^n states.

subject: automata
text: Context-Free Grammars and Pushdown Automata Context-Free Grammars (CFGs) generate the class of context-free languages, which strictly subsume regular languages. A CFG is a 4-tuple (V, Sigma, R, S), where V is a finite set of non-terminal variables, Sigma is the terminal alphabet, R is a finite set of production rules of the form A -> alpha with A in V and alpha in (V union Sigma)*, and S is the start symbol. A Pushdown Automaton (PDA) is the mechanical equivalent of a CFG. It extends a finite state machine with an unbounded Last-In-First-Out (LIFO) stack storage. Deterministic Pushdown Automata (DPDAs) recognize deterministic context-free languages, which form a strict subset of context-free languages recognized by non-deterministic PDAs (e.g., the language of palindromes {w w^R}).

text: Turing Machines and the Halting Problem A Turing Machine (TM) is a formal model of computation introduced by Alan Turing in 1936. It consists of an infinite memory tape divided into cells and a read/write tape head. The transition function delta maps Q x Gamma to Q x Gamma x {L, R}, where Gamma is the tape alphabet. The Church-Turing thesis states that any algorithm or effectively calculable function can be simulated by a Turing machine. The Halting Problem asks whether a given Turing machine M will halt on a specific input string w. Turing proved that the language A_TM = {<M, w> | M is a Turing Machine and M halts on input w} is undecidable using a diagonal argument. If a decider H for the halting problem existed, one could construct an adversarial machine D that reverses H's decision on its own description, yielding an insurmountable logical contradiction (D halts if and only if D does not halt).

subject: computer_networks
text: Computer Networks: Transport Layer Protocols and TCP 3-Way Handshake The Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) is a connection-oriented, reliable, byte-stream transport layer protocol defined in RFC 793. Unlike UDP, which is connectionless and best-effort, TCP provides guaranteed in-order delivery, flow control, and congestion control. Before data transfer begins, TCP establishes a virtual connection between client and server using a Three-Way Handshake: 1. SYN: The active client generates a randomly chosen Initial Sequence Number (ISN_client = x) and sends a TCP segment with the SYN control flag set to 1. 2. SYN-ACK: The passive server receives the SYN segment, allocates connection buffers and state variables, generates its own Initial Sequence Number (ISN_server = y), and transmits a segment with SYN=1 and ACK=1, where the acknowledgment number is set to x + 1. 3. ACK: The client receives the SYN-ACK, transitions to the ESTABLISHED state, and transmits an ACK segment with ACK=1 and acknowledgment number set to y + 1. Data payloads can accompany this third packet.

subject: computer_networks
text: TCP Flow Control vs Congestion Control It is vital to distinguish between flow control and congestion control in computer networks: - Flow Control is a speed-matching service that prevents a fast sender from overwhelming a slow receiver's buffer space. TCP implements flow control using a receive window (`rwnd`) field in the TCP header. The receiver explicitly informs the sender of how many spare bytes of buffer space are currently available (`rwnd = RcvBuffer - [LastByteRcvd - LastByteRead]`). The sender ensures that the unacknowledged data never exceeds `rwnd`. - Congestion Control prevents senders from injecting too much traffic into the network subnet, avoiding packet loss and queue collapse in intermediate routers. TCP maintains a congestion window (`cwnd`). The effective transmission window is $\min(\text{cwnd}, \text{rwnd})$. TCP congestion control algorithms (such as TCP Reno and Tahoe) employ four phases: Slow Start (exponential window growth), Congestion Avoidance (additive increase / multiplicative decrease, AIMD), Fast Retransmit, and Fast Recovery.

subject: computer_networks
text: OSI Reference Model vs TCP/IP Protocol Stack The Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) reference model, developed by the International Organization for Standardization (ISO), is a conceptual framework with seven distinct architectural layers: 1. Physical Layer: Transmission and reception of raw unstructured bit streams over physical media. 2. Data Link Layer: Node-to-node frame transfer, media access control (MAC), and error detection (CRC). 3. Network Layer: Multi-hop routing, packet forwarding, and logical addressing (IPv4, IPv6). 4. Transport Layer: End-to-end process-to-process communication, multiplexing (TCP, UDP). 5. Session Layer: Dialog control, token management, and synchronization checkpoints. 6. Presentation Layer: Syntax translation, character encoding, data compression, and encryption/SSL. 7. Application Layer: High-level network application services (HTTP, DNS, SMTP, FTP). In contrast, the practical TCP/IP Internet model consolidates the top three layers into a single Application Layer, resulting in a streamlined four-layer stack: Network Interface (Link), Internet (IP), Transport (TCP/UDP), and Application.

text: Database Management Systems: ACID Transactions and Concurrency Control A transaction in a database management system is a logical unit of database processing that includes one or more database access operations. Transactions must satisfy the ACID properties: 1. Atomicity: Either all operations of the transaction are executed and reflected in the database, or none are. Handled by the write-ahead logging (WAL) recovery manager. 2. Consistency: Execution of a transaction in isolation preserves database consistency invariants and integrity constraints. 3. Isolation: Even if multiple transactions execute concurrently, the system guarantees that for every pair of transactions T_i and T_j, it appears to T_i that either T_j finished execution before T_i started, or T_j started execution after T_i finished. 4. Durability: Once a transaction successfully commits, the updates made to the database persist even in the event of system crashes.

subject: dbms
text: Two-Phase Locking (2PL) and Serializability Serializability is the standard criterion for the correctness of concurrent transaction execution. A concurrent schedule is conflict serializable if it is conflict equivalent to some serial schedule, which can be verified by constructing a precedence (or serialization) graph: a schedule is conflict serializable if and only if its precedence graph has no directed cycles. The Two-Phase Locking (2PL) protocol is a concurrency control mechanism that guarantees conflict serializability. Under basic 2PL: - Growing Phase: A transaction may acquire locks (shared or exclusive), but cannot release any lock. - Shrinking Phase: A transaction may release locks, but cannot acquire any new lock. Strict 2PL further requires that all exclusive locks held by a transaction be released only after the transaction commits or aborts, which prevents cascading rollbacks. Rigorous 2PL requires both shared and exclusive locks to be held until commit.

text: Relational Database Normalization: 1NF to BCNF Normalization is the systematic design process of organizing data to eliminate insertion, update, and deletion anomalies while minimizing data redundancy. - First Normal Form (1NF): A relation is in 1NF if every attribute domain contains only atomic (indivisible) values and each row is unique. - Second Normal Form (2NF): A relation is in 2NF if it is in 1NF and no non-prime attribute is partially dependent on any candidate key. - Third Normal Form (3NF): A relation is in 3NF if it is in 2NF and no non-prime attribute is transitively dependent on candidate keys (for every functional dependency X -> A, either X is a superkey or A is a prime attribute). - Boyce-Codd Normal Form (BCNF): A stricter version of 3NF where for every non-trivial functional dependency X -> A, X must be a superkey.

subject: operating_systems
text: Operating Systems: Process Synchronization and Deadlocks In multiprogramming environments, concurrent access to shared data can lead to data inconsistency. A race condition arises when several processes access and manipulate the same data concurrently and the outcome depends on the particular order in which access takes place. The critical-section problem requires three structural conditions to be satisfied: 1. Mutual Exclusion: If process P_i is executing in its critical section, then no other processes can be executing in their critical sections. 2. Progress: If no process is executing in its critical section and there exist some processes that wish to enter their critical section, then only those processes not executing in their remainder sections can participate in deciding which will enter next. 3. Bounded Waiting: There must be a bound on the number of times other processes are allowed to enter their critical sections after a process has made a request to enter and before that request is granted.

subject: operating_systems
text: Coffman's Four Conditions for Deadlock A deadlock is a state in which each process in a set is waiting for an event that only another process in the set can cause. Edward G. Coffman Jr. formalized that a deadlock situation can arise if and only if all four of the following conditions hold simultaneously: 1. Mutual Exclusion: At least one resource must be held in a non-shareable mode (only one process can use the resource at a time). 2. Hold and Wait: A process must be currently holding at least one resource and requesting additional resources that are currently being held by other processes. 3. No Preemption: Resources cannot be forcibly preempted from a process; a resource can only be released voluntarily by the process holding it after completing its task. 4. Circular Wait: A closed chain of processes exists such that each process holds at least one resource needed by the next process in the chain (P_0 waits for resource held by P_1, ..., P_n waits for resource held by P_0).

subject: operating_systems
text: Virtual Memory and Page Replacement Algorithms Virtual memory decouples the user's logical memory from physical memory, allowing execution of processes whose address spaces exceed available physical RAM. Memory is organized into fixed-size blocks called pages (in logical memory) and frames (in physical memory). When a process attempts to access a page not currently residing in physical RAM, the memory management unit (MMU) generates a page fault hardware interrupt. When a page fault occurs and all memory frames are occupied, a page replacement algorithm must select a victim frame to swap out: - FIFO (First-In, First-Out): Replaces the oldest page loaded in memory. Can suffer from Belady's Anomaly, where increasing the number of page frames results in an increased number of page faults. - Optimal (OPT / Belady's Min): Replaces the page that will not be used for the longest period of time in the future. Provides the lowest page fault rate but is impossible to implement in practice because future references cannot be known. - Least Recently Used (LRU): Replaces the page that has not been used for the longest period in the past. Approximates the optimal algorithm by using past temporal locality.
